title: Why Asking a Lot From Team Members Makes Them More Committed
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues, using the Pygmalion Effect, that leaders who pair high expectations with genuine relational care get more from their teams, not less, than those who lower demands out of fear of losing people. It uses the college athletics transfer portal as a case study, noting that the best coaches keep asking a lot of players despite the ease of leaving, because shared sacrifice builds commitment and closeness. The piece extends that lesson to ordinary workplace leaders, who have effectively always operated in an open transfer portal, arguing the answer to retention fears is to raise expectations while deepening genuine care, not to lower the bar.
points: The Pygmalion Effect is used to argue high expectations plus genuine care outperform lowered demands.
College coaches facing the transfer portal illustrate that demanding more, not less, builds player commitment.
Workplace leaders are said to have always faced an equivalent 'open transfer portal' with employees.
The prescribed fix for retention fears is raising expectations while investing more in relationships, not easing up.
quotes: Leaders with high standards and expectations, and who are relationally supportive of team members, amplify motivation, confidence, and commitment in those who follow them.
Psychologists call this the Pygmalion Effect after the Greek myth of a sculptor whose belief in the beauty of his statue brought it to life.
Many coaches are cautious about asking too much from players because they fear the players might pick up and go elsewhere. But the best college coaches do the opposite.
Leaders who are not college athletic coaches don’t normally think of it this way, but they have always operated in an open transfer portal.
The answer to this challenge is not to lower expectations and demands but to raise them.
